# Field Guide: Preparing a Home for a 72-Hour Power Outage

Prepare an ordinary household to get through a power outage of up to seventy-two hours safely and comfortably. It assumes a temperate climate and no backup generator. Work through the sections in order; earlier sections matter most.

## Water

Store four litres of water per person per day — twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours. Half is for drinking, half for cooking and basic hygiene. Use food-grade containers, keep them out of direct sunlight, and replace stored water every six months. If a storm is forecast and you have warning, also fill the bathtub; bathtub water is for flushing toilets and washing, never drinking.

## Food

Keep a dedicated shelf of non-perishable food for three days: canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, and shelf-stable milk. Choose foods needing no cooking, and own a manual can opener, since an electric one will be useless. Eat perishable refrigerator food first, then freezer food, and only then the emergency shelf.

## Refrigerator and freezer

An unopened refrigerator keeps food safe about four hours. A full freezer holds a safe temperature about forty-eight hours, but a half-full one only about twenty-four, so keep the freezer consolidated and full — even with containers of frozen water. Keep both doors closed as much as possible and tape a reminder note to each. Discard any perishable food left more than two hours above four degrees Celsius; when in doubt, throw it out.

## Light

Use battery-powered LED lanterns or headlamps as your primary light, and avoid candles entirely, since they are a leading cause of house fires during outages. Store at least one light per person plus two spare sets of batteries for each. Keep one headlamp beside each bed and one lantern in the kitchen, placed where they can be found in the dark.

## Heat and safety

Never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator indoors, in a garage, or near a window; each produces carbon monoxide, which is odourless and can be fatal. Install at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on each floor where people sleep. In cold weather, pick one small room on the home's south-facing side, close its door, and gather everyone there; layered clothing and blankets are safer than any improvised heater. If the indoor temperature falls below ten degrees Celsius and you cannot stay warm, relocate to a warming centre or a neighbour's home.

## Communication and information

Keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio for emergency broadcasts, and learn your local emergency station's frequency before the outage. Charge every phone and power bank whenever a storm is forecast; a full twenty-thousand-milliamp-hour power bank recharges a typical phone roughly four times. Put your phone in low-power mode at the start. Agree in advance on one out-of-area contact whom every household member will text, since texts get through congested networks more reliably than voice calls.

## Medical needs

Keep a first-aid kit and a seven-day supply of every prescription medication, rotating them to stay in date. Refrigerated medication such as insulin generally stays usable at room temperature up to twenty-eight days, but confirm the rule for your specific medication with a pharmacist beforehand. Write your pharmacy, doctor, and poison-control numbers on paper, because a dead phone is not a phone book.

## When the power returns

Wait five minutes before switching major appliances back on, letting the grid stabilise. Check the freezer: food still holding ice crystals can be safely refrozen. Restock everything used within one week, starting with water and batteries. Finally, write a one-page note on what was missing or awkward, and fix at least one gap before the next outage.
hardConstraintNote: Still a self-contained instruction document: all eight original sections retained with their headers and original order (Water, Food, Refrigerator and freezer, Light, Heat and safety, Communication and information, Medical needs, When the power returns), every instruction is a standalone imperative a reader can act on with no external reference, and every load-bearing quantity, duration, temperature, item list, and ordered sequence is preserved. Nothing points outside the document.

rationale: One prose-tightening pass over all 8 sections. Removed opener throat-clearing ('This guide explains how to prepare...'), collapsed the water restatement ('four litres per person per day, which means twelve litres') into an em-dash apposition, converted passives to active ('should be discarded' -> 'Discard'), and trimmed connective filler ('so it is worth keeping', 'even if some of the space is taken up by'). Every numeric fact, item in every list, and ordered step survives verbatim in meaning; only redundancy and padding are cut. Conservative relative to the ~560-word line-editor ceiling because I refused to shed any gate-relevant fact or restructure sentences into fragments (that is the restructurer's lens, not mine). Result: 730 -> 618, ~15% off, with all ~40 facts intact -- the correct posture given I am BLIND to which 8 the Gap will probe (T2/GR-4), so preserving ALL content is the only winning play.
title: Sentence-level tightening: cut throat-clearing, restatement, and connective padding; passive to active
